q: I want every file changed in the last 24 hours. Do I use -mtime 1 or -mtime -1?
expl: -mtime -1 means less than one day old. Plain 1 means one to two days old.

q: README.md is 47 hours old. Will find . -type f -mtime +1 list it?
expl: No. 47 hours rounds down to one whole day, and 1 is not greater than 1. -mmin +1440 has no rounding.
opts: No: it needs two full days; use -mmin +1440

q: Type a `find` command that lists the regular files (`-type f`) in the current folder changed in the last 2 hours. Count in minutes.
expl: `-mmin -120` means less than 120 minutes ago. Unlike `-mtime`, minutes give you exact limits.

q: In the demo folder (README.md is 47 hours old, old_notes.txt 50 hours, LICENSE 5 days), what does this print?
expl: `+1` means at least two full days after the fraction is dropped, so README.md (47 h = 1 day) is not listed.

q: Type the command that lists files changed in the last 24 hours (use `-mmin -1440`), skips `./node_modules` completely, and does not print the folder itself.
expl: `-prune` stops find from going into the folder; `-print` at the end makes sure only the right side of `-o` is printed.

q: You run `find . -path ./node_modules -prune -o -type f -mmin -1440` (no `-print` at the end). What's wrong with the result?
expl: With no action anywhere, find prints everything that matched, and the pruned path matched the left side of `-o`.
opts: Files inside node_modules are still listed
The `./node_modules` folder itself appears in the list

q: What does this print in the demo folder? (utils.py is 30 hours old, README.md 47 hours.)
expl: The window is “newer than 2 days ago” AND NOT “newer than 1 day ago”: between 24 and 48 hours old.
show: find . -type f -newermt '2 days ago' ! -newermt '1 day ago' | sort

q: Which test matches files older than exactly 24 hours, with no rounding?
expl: 1440 minutes is exactly 24 hours. `-mtime +1` skips files between 24 and 48 hours old.

q: Type a command that runs `ls -l` on every file changed in the last 2 hours (`-mmin -120`), with a single `ls` call (`-exec … +`).
expl: `-exec … {} +` collects all the names and runs the command once; `{} \;` would start one `ls` per file.

q: Why pipe `find -print0` into `tar --null -T -` instead of the plain list of names?
expl: `-print0` ends every name with a null byte, the one character a file name can't contain.
opts: A file name with a newline (or other odd characters) can't break the list
tar can't read file names from a pipe without it
